Overview

John James was an anti-abortion extremist who declared he was “100% pro-life” and compared abortion to “genocide.”

John James supported the overturning of Roe v. Wade, claimed “life begins at conception,” and opposed abortion exceptions for rape and incest. He pledged to only support judges who supported abortion restrictions. While in Congress, John James voted to ban the abortion drug Mifepristone. 

John James supported efforts to defund Planned Parenthood and eliminating federal funding for abortion providers. 

In June 2026, John James visited and praised the Pregnancy Resource Center of Grand Rapids, an anti-abortion clinic that stated it did not offer, recommend, or refer patients for abortions. Medical experts at the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists warned that crisis pregnancy centers could deter patients from seeking certain reproductive health care options, including abortion care.

James has long aligned himself with the anti-abortion movement. He maintained deep ties with Right to Life of Michigan, which financially supported his campaigns and promoted their extreme anti-abortion movement. James also received backing from the anti-abortion Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, including its endorsement and an A+ rating. James promoted the March for Life and praised young activists who traveled to Washington, D.C. to “stand up for life.”

John James Voted For A Ban On The Sale Of Mifepristone In The FY 2024 Agriculture Appropriations Bill

John James Voted For The FY 2024 Agriculture Appropriations Bill That Targeted Mifepristone Access

2023: John James Voted For Passing FY 2024 Agriculture Appropriations Bill Which Targeted Mifepristone Access. In September 2023, John James voted for: “Passage of the bill that would provide roughly $22 billion in discretionary funding in fiscal 2024 for the Agriculture Department and related agencies. The bill would provide $6.2 billion to the Food and Drug Administration, including $3 billion in discretionary budget authority and $3.2 billion in user fees; $3.4 billion for Agriculture Department rural development activities; $1.5 billion for the Agricultural Research Service; and $1 billion for the Food Safety and Inspection Service. It would provide $122 billion for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, $32 billion for child nutrition programs, and $6 billion for the Women, Infants, and Children program. It would direct the USDA to take necessary actions to prohibit the purchase of U.S. agricultural land by non-resident aliens and foreign businesses associated with Russia, North Korea, Iran and China; nullify the FDA’s January 2023 rule allowing medical providers to dispense the abortion drug mifepristone without an in-person consultation; prohibit the use of funds for programs that promote critical race theory; and prohibit the use of funds to establish any office of diversity, equity and inclusion, among other policy provisions. As amended, the bill would prohibit the use of funds for carrying out various Biden administration executive orders related to climate change and sex discrimination, finalizing regulations that result in an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more, implementing the USDA COVID-19 workplace safety policy, or for any operations of the Civilian Climate Corps, among other restrictions. It also would reduce the salary of Deputy Undersecretary of Agriculture for Food and Nutrition Service Stacy Dean to $1.” The bill was rejected by a vote of 191-237. [H.R. 4368, Vote #507, 9/28/25]

  • The FY 2024 Agriculture Appropriations Bill Included A Provision To Ban Mifepristone From Being Sold In Retail Pharmacies Or By Mail. According to Fox 59, “A provision in the legislation would nullify a Biden administration rule allowing mifepristone to be sold in retail pharmacies and by mail with prescriptions from a certified health care provider.” [Fox 59, 9/27/23]
  • Planned Parenthood: “‘Abortion Pill’ Is The Common Name For Using Two Different Medicines To End A Pregnancy: Mifepristone And Misoprostol.” According to Planned Parenthood, “‘Abortion pill’ is the common name for using two different medicines to end a pregnancy: mifepristone and misoprostol. You can also use misoprostol alone to have an abortion. First, you take a pill called mifepristone. Pregnancy needs a hormone called progesterone to grow normally. Mifepristone blocks your body’s own progesterone, stopping the pregnancy from growing. Then you take the second medicine, misoprostol, either right away or up to 48 hours later. This medicine causes cramping and bleeding to empty your uterus. It’s kind of like having a really heavy, crampy period, and the process is very similar to an early miscarriage. If you don’t have any bleeding within 24 hours after taking misoprostol, call your nurse or doctor.” [Planned Parenthood -  The Abortion Pill, Accessed 11/5/25]

The American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists Warned That Crisis Pregnancy Centers Were Unregulated Facilities That Could Mislead Patients And Delay Access To Reproductive Health Care

The American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists: Crisis Pregnancy Centers (CPC) Worked To Deter People From Seeking Certain Reproductive Health Care Options. According to The American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists, "People seeking reproductive health care must have access to comprehensive, evidence-based, nonjudgmental health care and information from qualified professionals, regardless of whether they decide to continue a pregnancy or seek abortion care. It’s important that people understand their options and know their resources—including how to recognize and avoid facilities, such as crisis pregnancy centers (CPCs), run by people who operate unethically and with the intention to dissuade, deter, or prevent them from seeking certain reproductive health care options.” [American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists, Issues Brief: Crisis Pregnancy Centers, Archived 6/18/26]

The American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists: Crisis Pregnancy Centers Often Operated As Unregulated Facilities That Were Not Subject To HIPAA Requirements And Had No Legal Obligation To Provide Accurate Information To Patients. According to The American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists, "CPC is a term used to refer to certain facilities that represent themselves as legitimate reproductive health care clinics providing care for pregnant people but actually aim to dissuade people from accessing certain types of reproductive health care, including abortion care and even contraceptive options. Staff members at these unregulated and often nonmedical facilities have no legal obligation to provide pregnant people with accurate information and are not subject to HIPAA or required by law to maintain client confidentiality. Many CPCs are affiliated with national organizations that provide funding, support, and training to advance a broadscale antiabortion agenda.” [American College Of Obstetricians And Gynecologists, Issues Brief: Crisis Pregnancy Centers, Archived 6/18/26]
